books: Destrehan Plantation (French: Plantation Destrehan; Spanish: Plantación Destrehan) is an antebellum mansion in the French colonial style modified with Greek Revival architectural elements. It is located in southeast Louisiana, near the town of Destrehan, about 22 miles west of New Orleans. It was established during the period of Spanish rule (once occupied by French until 1763) between 1787 and 1790, which heavily integrated building styles and structural strategies adapted from Saint-Domingue (Haiti) by the French and Cuba by the Spanish, between the migration networks were deeply tied.

During the 19th century, the plantation was a major producer of indigo and then sugarcane. The home is most commonly associated with its second owner, Jean-Noël Destréhan, who served briefly as the first United States senator from Louisiana in 1812. He was influential in the transition of the Orleans Territory to statehood.
The house is a unique example of a plantation home outliving the oil refinery that had been built around it. It is listed on the National Register of Historic Places for its architectural quality and association with important people and events in the history of both Louisiana and Mississippi along the Mississippi River that ties to Haitian Vodou.
